Verified Agentic Engineering in PracticeA component system grown from 55 to 229 components in one month - what the gates caught, what they missed, and what it cost

  • Aron Homberg1
  • 1independent researcher - defuss open-source project

Method and data: Aron Homberg. Text: Claude (Opus 5.5), the coding agent, in a Claude Code session run under the method. Section 10 is the agent's own position.

defuss-vae Code ARCH.md Slides Issues

DataEvery current figure on this page is measured on each build and checked by the verifier it describes. Historical figures are read from git and the issue tracker and dated 2026-10-05; the session of section 5.6 is read from its transcript, dated 2026-10-06.

Abstract

Coding agents write interface code faster than a person can review it, and every change risks an invariant nobody wrote down. Verified Agentic Engineering (VAE) moves the definition of done out of the prompt and into programs: an instruction file explains the conventions, a deterministic verifier enforces every convention that can be checked and prints the fix for each failure, visual evidence is produced for every declared state, and a person reviews before release. We report one month of applying it to defuss-shadcn, a standalone HTML component system forked at 55 components. In 28 days, 191 commits and 281,692 added lines of authored code (73,104 removed, the fork's import included) the system grew to 229 components across 15 releases, while one command - 78 gates in 10.2 s - kept it consistent. Code, once committed, rarely came back out: 3.7 % of the lines added to components, tests and the shared runtime were removed again. The most practical result is a single session: one requirement - typed, fully documented APIs - applied consistently to all 59 interactive components in four hours, held together by the gate. A second change in the same session raised unit-test line coverage by 44 percentage points - 31.6 % to 75.6 %, 10,420 more lines covered - in 21 minutes and 39,926 output tokens, with 147 lines of tests. A third moved all 228 component folders into the 19 sections of the sidebar, under a new gate, in 43 minutes. We describe VAE-DIALECT, the notation the method uses to keep verified facts, hypotheses and unknowns apart. We also report, as anecdotes, what the gates did not catch: a build that froze the maintainer's machine, an animation timing bug, a growth claim the data did not support. Section 10 is the position of the agent that wrote this report; the last section names the research still open.

1Introduction

A prompt can ask an agent to run the tests, to mock nothing and to remove its debug output. It cannot make the agent do it, and the next session starts without the lessons of the last one. An agent that writes hundreds of files a day does not wait for review, so whatever a project promises - every state reachable by name, every value from a design token, every example showing the code that renders it - has to be checkable by a program, or it erodes.

VAE is a response to that. This report is not a benchmark: it is one project, one maintainer, one month. Its value is that everything in it can be checked. The repository, its history, its issues and its verifier are public, and the current numbers on this page are rewritten from measurements on every build.

2The method

VAE, as packaged in defuss-vae, has five human-triggered skills - plan, implement, review, docs, finalize - and small stdlib-only programs that verify, gate and remember. The agent does the work; programs decide whether the work is done.

2.1 Programs, not prompts

Hooks deny git commit until the exact code fingerprint has passed verify, review and docs, and send the agent back when it tries to stop early. The gate fails closed: a missing command, a missing metric or a crashing check blocks instead of waving the change through. Tests use real subsystems instead of mocks; end-to-end tests consume the built artifact and must leave fresh output. A check that cannot fail is not evidence - the defuss-vae notes record that plain oxlint exits 0 on findings, which is why every lint call carries --deny-warnings.

VERIFIED (defuss-vae 0.5.3 source) Each project owns its policy in .agents/VERIFY.py: the command behind each verb, the thresholds, and rules the gate executes on every run. The agent extends it: a defect class that can recur becomes a rule there or a test. The first rule an agent added here was a workaround, and it exposed a gap on both sides: the plugin's CI template assumed a bootstrap this repository does not provide, and a verifier that needs screenshots generated locally, so the agent kept the template out instead of fixing either. The repository then had no CI at all; it has had its own workflow since 2026-10-06, which generates the screenshots before it verifies - green on its third run - and the rule is gone. The plugin side is its author's to change. The gate is lean on purpose: it caches a green run under a hash of the code and the policy, and a second one for the doc pages, so a typo fixed in a page after green suites reruns only the page checks, and the review and documentation steps rerun nothing. Inside the suites, this repository's e2e runner adds its own selection - only the files whose inputs changed run.

2.2 Memory that is loaded

Failures become episodes; recurring ones become tests or verifier rules; durable decisions go into a short memory file that the harness injects into every new session. Lessons are ranked by strength: an executable check > a memory line > an episode line. The strongest form of a lesson is one a program enforces, because a model forgets and a gate does not.

VERIFIED (defuss-vae 0.5.3 source) The agent's state lives in the repository, in .agents/: MEMORY.md (durable decisions and constraints, at most 4 KiB), CLI_GIST.md (the shortest working commands, at most 2 KiB, tagged VERIFIED only after an observed success) and EPISODES.md, where the gate itself writes every FAIL and every distinct finding. A session start - and a context compaction - loads the rules, the memory, the gist and the recent episodes. The agent may also change AGENTS.md, within limits: it adds a rule only to prevent a repeated mistake, removes its own rule once a test or verifier rule enforces it, and never deletes what a person wrote - it proposes that change instead. Finalizing audits every entry against the current code and deletes or rewrites only on evidence.

2.3 Prose that is checked

Agents write documentation in a recognizable machine voice - em dashes everywhere, typographic quotes, the ellipsis character, confident claims without a source. defuss-vae treats documentation pages like code. VERIFIED (defuss-vae 0.5.3 source) Every changed page passes a static check for machine-writing tells, invisible and look-alike characters, broken links, leftover placeholders and Mermaid diagrams that would not render. A dash is never swapped for another character: the sentence is rewritten by meaning, as a comma, a colon, parentheses or two sentences. A catalog review then reads for what only reading catches - whether a claim has its evidence, whether a conclusion follows, whether a number has its base - and the gate requires a documentation attestation for the exact code fingerprint, with every material claim tagged VERIFIED, HYPOTHESIS or UNKNOWN.

VERIFIED On this repository's 605 documentation pages the static check found 380 findings at the last commit before the session of section 5.6: 198 dashes (191 em dashes, 7 spaced en dashes), 181 typographic characters (132 ellipsis characters, 37 curly apostrophes, 12 curly quotes) and one broken link. After that session's documentation pass it finds none, and this page passes it too.

3VAE-DIALECT

VAE-DIALECT is a superset of technical English for agent output and for the skills' own prompts: fewer tokens, still uniquely decodable. Its rule of precedence is short - correctness > compression. Its core is three epistemic tags that never mix:

  • VERIFIED[scope] Established by direct inspection, command output, a test, a measurement or a named authoritative source. Evidence older than the last relevant edit is stale.
  • HYPOTHESIS[scope] A testable inference, not yet established - with the cheapest discriminating test or falsifier when it matters.
  • UNKNOWN[scope] A material fact the available evidence does not establish - naming the missing evidence. P=? marks an unknown value.

Confidence language never promotes a hypothesis. On top of the tags, a small operator grammar replaces whole phrases. Operators are exact uppercase words; any other uppercase is forbidden, so an operator is never ambiguous:

Why uppercase. HYPOTHESIS uppercase operators hold a model's attention where the logic of a sentence sits, so an operator is read as an operator. Dillitzer et al. (Attention is Case-Sensitive, 2026) support the mechanism: across 13 models, uppercase spans in lowercase text concentrate the model's attention on them, in every non-reasoning model they evaluated. They also bound it - more attention did not by itself raise accuracy, and the thinking phase of reasoning models damped the effect - so the study supports that the operators are noticed, not that they are understood better. Falsifier: equal error rates with uppercase operators, with lowercase ones and with none, on a reasoning and a non-reasoning model.

Its losslessness rule is what makes it more than shorthand: before emitting compressed text, the writer expands it mentally; if the expansion is not unique, or loses more than negligible meaning, the shortest longer form that is unique is used instead. A report in the dialect reads like this:

VERIFIED[bundle] BC `bun tests/e2e/scaffold-lean.e2e.ts` → 6/6 apps render as on all.css + all.js
HYPOTHESIS[leak] BC heap +36 MB/page after module release; falsifier=close each happy-dom window, re-measure
UNKNOWN[scaffold-time] BC no timestamps in this repo for the prompts that built the scaffolds
IF HYPOTHESIS[leak] THEN next=cap heap at 4 GB, probe ELSE next=bisect plugins

4The case: defuss-shadcn

defuss-shadcn is a component system of semantic HTML, modern CSS and plain JavaScript on shadcn/ui's design tokens: no framework, no build step for consumers. It was forked from codylindley/shadcn-html, which had 55 component folders when its development stopped in April 2026. The fork's first commit is dated 2026-09-05.

The project applies the method with its own tools rather than the defuss-vae plugin, which was published later, on 2026-10-01: an instruction file (AGENTS.md) and a verifier (scripts/verify.ts) that runs at the end of every build. Its gates cover, among others: a 1:1 compile of the sources; the State API every interactive component must expose - states by name, a store, and render() reproducing the authored markup exactly, proven by an end-to-end contract; schemas that must match each page's state table row for row; DOM access only through one runtime; screenshots for every declared state in light and dark; and every number a page claims, written from its measurement. The same rules run on these very pages.

VERIFIED Since 2026-10-06 the defuss-vae gate wraps that verifier (.agents/VERIFY.py): lint, the unit tests, a coverage floor that may only rise, verify and the end-to-end suite must pass, then a review and a documentation attestation are written for the exact code fingerprint - only then is a commit allowed. Section 5.6 is the first session run under it.

5.1 Growth

VERIFIED From git, at the last commit of each week (Monday to Sunday): 55 components and 5 e2e files on the first day, 2026-09-05; then, week by week, 55 and 56 (Aug 31–Sep 6), 72 and 75 (Sep 7–13), 72 and 78 (Sep 14–20), 77 and 83 (Sep 21–27) and 219 and 231 (Sep 28–Oct 4) - and 229 components with 242 e2e files in the working tree on 2026-10-05. In the same span the verifier's check groups grew from 33 to 41; each runs over every component, which is how 41 groups report 78 gates.

VERIFIED Across the same commits, 281,692 lines were added and 73,104 removed in authored files (git --numstat; generated output - dist/, docs/, the compiled docs runtime, the generated skills, lockfiles, screenshots - excluded). The first week (Aug 31–Sep 6) carries 70,742 of them, 56,640 on its first day, 2026-09-05: that is mostly the forked codebase entering the repository, not a day's work. Removals cluster in the documentation (65,582 of 73,104), the largest on 2026-09-11 (35,380 lines), when the static HTML pages moved to an MDX site generator. Tests grew by 47,230 lines while components grew by 71,693 - about 66 test lines per 100 component lines. The working tree on 2026-10-05, the session that wrote this report, adds 44,710 and removes 2,492 more, uncommitted.

5.2 Review load

VERIFIED On 2026-09-07 the maintainer reviewed the documentation site by hand and filed 52 issues in about eight hours - wrong corners, missing examples, unannounced field hints, dead links. 18 were closed within twelve hours; the fix commits name their issues (fix(select): … (issue #32)). The remaining ones were closed in one batch on 2026-09-28, so for those the close date is an upper bound, not the fix date.

That sweep is the human review the method budgets for: one person reading what the gates cannot judge - whether a corner looks right - instead of re-checking what they can. HYPOTHESIS the review effort per component falls as the gates grow, because each class of defect found by hand becomes a gate; falsifier: issue counts per new component that do not fall across sweeps. One sweep is not enough data to say.

5.3 What it ships

Every component is measured on each build: 169 of 229 need no JavaScript. The whole system is 266.3 KiB as one bundle (minified and gzipped); a real application ships a fraction. Each application scaffold is bundled on its own - the core plus only the components its markup uses - and an end-to-end test proves it renders exactly as on the full bundle.

5.4 Generation speed

VERIFIED Aron Homberg SAYS each of the six application scaffolds took about 15 minutes to generate and was driven by a prompt of five to ten sentences. UNKNOWN for this report: the repository holds no timestamps of those prompts, so the figure is the maintainer's account, not a measurement. What the repository does show is that each scaffold passes the same gates as hand-reviewed components, its own interaction e2e, and the lean-bundle equivalence test.

HYPOTHESIS current frontier models build such applications quickly because the system gives them good examples (every component page is executable documentation) and clear instructions (a skill per component), and because the gate turns their mistakes into fix lines instead of silent drift. Falsifier: the same prompts against the same models without the component skills and without the verifier, timed and gated the same way. We have not run that comparison.

5.5 Churn

VERIFIED From Table 2: code that landed mostly stayed. Of the lines added to the components, 2,731 of 71,693 were removed again (3.8 %); tests 1,642 of 47,230 (3.5 %); the shared runtime 363 of 8,175 (4.4 %) - together 4,736 of 127,098, or 3.7 %. The project's removals sit elsewhere: 65,582 of its 73,104 removed lines are documentation, 35,380 of them on the single day the static pages moved to an MDX site generator - a planned migration, not rework. The tooling churns most among the code (1,547 of 7,440, 20.8 %), and it is the code the gates themselves live in, rewritten as they grew.

Two reasons, one established and one not. VERIFIED the architecture is additive: every component is a folder of its own (a skill, a stylesheet, a script) and shared behaviour sits in one runtime, so a new component adds files and edits none of its neighbours. HYPOTHESIS the gates keep defects out of commits, so code is not rewritten after it lands - a defect the verifier names is fixed before the commit, not in a follow-up that replaces the first attempt. Falsifier: line survival per commit (the age of each line in git blame) showing component code replaced within days of landing. We have not measured it.

5.6 A deep change in one session

Growth adds modules. The harder change - and the one agentic engineering has struggled with - runs through all of them: a new architectural rule or a general requirement that every module must follow, applied consistently across hundreds of modules so that the system still scales. An agent edits the first modules carefully and the later ones loosely, and nothing tells it which ones it missed. The session that added this section made exactly such a change, and the gate is what held it together.

The requirement, stated in two messages: every interactive component documents its API from typed source - a TypeScript signature for every member, a table for every argument, a typed and described detail for every event, the config each state accepts, and the shared State API (setState, getState, render, the store) typed for each component's own states - checked by the verifier, by the compiler and on every rendered page.

  • VERIFIED Every module, not a sample. By the final green gate, all 59 interactive component sources had changed (+3,455 / −408 lines); in all, 246 authored files (+7,570 / −1,537, generated output excluded - the session also built the section bundles and a documentation pass). verify's API docs gate reports no gap in any of the 59, and an end-to-end audit opens all 59 pages.
  • VERIFIED The written types are checked. A compiler ratchet counts type errors per file; it started at 1,212 and stood at 1,147 after this change; section 5.9 took it to 0, so any new wrong type fails the build.
  • VERIFIED It ran long. The whole session, up to the request for this section: 5.5 hours wall clock (4.8 hours without pauses over 15 minutes), 662 tool calls, 516,020 output tokens, and one compaction of the agent's context - the work continued from a summary without losing the requirement.
  • VERIFIED The tests stayed lean. The e2e runner reruns only the files whose inputs changed: 4 of 245 after a fix to two components, 135 after a change that touched every component.

What this establishes is narrow and solid. VERIFIED a deep, long-running change that every one of 59 modules must follow can be made consistently in one agent session, from a requirement in prose and without a module done by hand first, when a program checks every module - this session is the existence proof. It was not flawless: the first pass passed a gate that checked the source but not the pages, and a person caught it (section 7). HYPOTHESIS it repeats - other repositories, other requirements, other models. Falsifier: a change of the same kind under the same kind of gate that ends with modules the gate passes and a reviewer rejects. HYPOTHESIS the session stayed affordable because the tests ran lean and the agent's notes and memory are written in VAE-DIALECT; falsifier: the same session with every test on every step and plain-prose notes, measured the same way.

In 20.6 minutes and 39,926 output tokens, the agent raised unit-test line coverage by 44.0 percentage points - from 31.6 % to 75.6 %, 10,420 more lines of code executed by the suite (5,460 to 15,880) - with 147 lines of tests and an 11-line fix. VERIFIED (the session transcript and the coverage runs) Over the same window the model re-read 21.6 million tokens of cached context across its calls - the session's context, served from the prompt cache, not new work - took 86 fresh input tokens and wrote 58,198 tokens to the cache.

VERIFIED The second change was requested on 2026-10-06 at 13:08 UTC: the gate's coverage floor stood at 30 %, Vitest measured 31.6 % of lines, and the target was at least 60 % - another change across the whole system. Same session, same agent: Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, under the defuss-vae 0.5.3 gate. It went in two steps, each read from the session transcript and the coverage runs:

  • VERIFIED Step 1: one test, not hundreds. The agent did not write a test per uncovered line. Every interactive component already had an end-to-end fixture with every documented configuration; one contract test loads all 63 interactive fixtures - the 59 components' and four that compose them - in the unit suite and drives every bound element through every declared state: getState(), the store and render() must agree, and an undeclared name must throw. Four minutes after the request: 66.9 %.
  • VERIFIED It found a defect on its first run. 58 of the 59 components passed. The cookie consent's controller replaces el.api and lacked settled(), which the State API promises on every element - fixed in 11 lines.
  • VERIFIED Step 2: every control, operated. Asked to go higher where it pays most, the agent reused the same fixtures once more: one more test clicks every control, sends the keys a keyboard user would and edits every field, holding each component to its main error path - no handler throws, no promise rejects unhandled. It passed on its first run, 63 of 63, and lifted lines to 75.6 % and branches from 38.6 % to 50.5 %. Both tests together are 147 lines.
  • VERIFIED Where it stopped, and why. The largest gaps left are the documentation site's own runtime (about 560 lines, not shipped), third-party packages (about 660) and specific paths in a few large components - each further point there costs a test written for one module. Browser-mode coverage counts what the pages load, third-party packages included (excluding them had no effect in this mode), so the figure is conservative. The gate's floor is now 70 %, and it may only rise.

Where the first change was large in code, this one is large in reach and small in code. HYPOTHESIS it was this cheap because the first change had made the contract uniform and complete - every interactive component exposes the same documented State API, and every one has a fixture of every configuration, so two tests reach all of them. Falsifier: a system without such a contract reaching the same coverage at the same cost. Lesson for the method: before writing tests, look for the contract the modules already share, and for the fixtures that already exist.

In 43.4 minutes and 76,358 output tokens, the agent moved every one of the 228 component folders into the section of the sidebar that lists it, made the layout a rule the verifier enforces, and kept every gate green - 246 end-to-end files, 570 unit tests, the verifier - without a human correction. VERIFIED (the session transcript, git and the gate) Over the same window the model re-read 56.2 million tokens of cached context, took 172 fresh input tokens and wrote 130,876 tokens to the cache.

The request, at 15:44:52 UTC: the files on disk should read like the documentation's sidebar - a verifier rule that every component's skill names its section in the front matter (section: actions), a folder per section directly under src/components/, and every component moved into its section, so src/components/button becomes src/components/actions/button. A structural change to all components, and to everything that finds them: the build, the bundler, the screenshot tool, the API reader, the e2e planner, the docs components, the tests.

  • VERIFIED Every half-done state was a named failure. Git refused to move questionnaire into a section of the same name; the section plan read the half-moved tree and listed the new folders as components; the statistics crashed reading the flat dist/ through the new helper; the link gate found 481 dead links - 253 between skills, 228 in the generated index; the plugin's prose check refused an exception for the index, so the links were fixed at the source and flattened on the way to dist/; the type checker caught test fixtures without the new key; the configuration check caught two environment variables the touched scripts read. Each was fixed before the gate turned green.
  • VERIFIED The new rule fails when it should. A component without section:, a component in the wrong section and a component outside any section each fail the component sections gate, which names the git mv or the front-matter line that fixes it (a probe; tests/component-sections.test.ts pins each case).
  • VERIFIED Consumers see nothing. The minified sizes and the published paths are the same; only the unminified bundle grew by 0.6 KiB, because its comments name the longer source paths.

HYPOTHESIS a structural change across every module is cheap when one module owns the structure and every other asks it, and safe when the gates turn each half-done state into a named failure instead of a silent one - the agent never had to remember what it had not moved yet. Falsifier: the same move without the gates, or with each tool joining its own paths, taking longer or ending with a tool that still looks in the old place.

In 12.5 minutes and 71,958 output tokens, the agent removed all 1,147 type errors the compiler ratchet had carried in 52 component files; after 27.3 minutes and 82,855 tokens every gate was green again - the verifier, 571 unit tests, 246 end-to-end files - and the 85 minified files the system ships were byte for byte the same as before, without a human correction. VERIFIED (the session transcript, git, the compiler, cmp and the gate) Up to zero errors the model re-read 79.3 million tokens of cached context, took 178 fresh input tokens and wrote 135,450 tokens to the cache; up to the green gates, 91.6 million, 236 and 225,359.

The work began at 17:29:02 UTC, right after section 5.8: fix the errors the ratchet had counted since section 5.6, and measure again. Since then every written type has been checked, but only against a baseline that may fall and never rise. This change goes into the meaning of the code where 5.8 went into its place, and it must not change what runs: a type is erased by the build, so the shipped bytes are its proof.

  • VERIFIED The owner first. Every component selects the DOM through one shared module. Typing what it returns there - an HTMLElement by default, the named element for a tag selector - removed 707 of the 1,147 errors (a probe: the previous commit plus that one file). The other 440 were local: optional parameters, event targets, the shape of a state declared where it grows.
  • VERIFIED The byte comparison found a bug no type could. After the edits, the Notes app's bundle differed from before. The bundler finds the components an app needs by reading the source for their init calls, and dfDollar<HTMLDialogElement>('dialog:not(...)') no longer looked like one, so the Notes app would have shipped without the dialog script. Two verifier checks read the source the same way and failed by name: the State API marker for the tree view and the dialog ownership boundary. All three now accept a type argument, and tests/apps.test.ts pins the bundler's case. UNKNOWN whether an end-to-end test would have caught the missing script - the broken bundle never ran.
  • VERIFIED The compiler corrected the agent. The agent first typed the calendar's selected day as a string; the next compile named every place that calculates with it, and the type became number | null.

Lesson for the method: when a change must not alter behavior, compare the shipped bytes as well as running the tests - here the comparison was the only check that saw the missing script. And a tool that reads source as text is a parser of the language: new syntax in the source, here a type argument, is new input for every such tool.

HYPOTHESIS the fourth change was fast for the reason the third was: one module owns what every query returns, so a type fixed there is fixed in every component that asks it. Falsifier: removing the same errors component by component, without the shared fix, taking no more edits per error.

5.10 Small modules, clear contracts

HYPOTHESIS VAE works this well here because every module stands on its own. Microservices, micro-frontends and small components suit an agent better than a person: a person drowns in hundreds of components, while an agent reads any one of them in full, and a gate can check every one of them on every run. The agent does not hold the whole system in mind either - this session's context was compacted once - it does not need to: each module can be read alone, and the gate holds the whole. The risk sits between modules. Where a contract between two of them is implicit or keeps changing, a test the agent saw green can turn red after the next, unrelated change, and nothing names the dependency that broke. Under VAE, separation of concerns, explicit contracts, small modules and composition over inheritance or shared dependencies are therefore not style - they are what makes a green gate mean something.

  • VERIFIED Explicit contracts. Every component is a folder of its own, and every interactive one exposes a contract a program checks: states by name, a store, a render() that reproduces its markup, a schema, a typed API. Because each end-to-end test's inputs are explicit, the runner can pick the tests a change affects - 4 of 245 after a fix to two components.
  • VERIFIED Three failures came from the gaps between modules. The docs search palette went dead because the dialog script claimed a <dialog> that another component owned; it is now an explicit ownership rule and a gate. In the session of section 5.6 the tabs script claimed the BibTeX component's tablist - found only when each section was bundled on its own. And every live example made the page recalculate its styles once per example: a cost no single module showed, only many of them on one page (section 6).

Falsifier: changes that cross module boundaries breaking green tests no more often than changes inside one module. The repository can measure it - which commits fix a test that an earlier commit left green, and how many component folders each touches - and we have not measured it yet.

6Anecdotes: self-correction

This section and the next are anecdotes: cases from a few sessions, chosen because each shows a mechanism, not counted or sampled. The representative evidence is the product itself - section 5, measured over every component on every build. The most useful thing a gate does is not to fail - it is to make the agent's next step obvious. Agents in VAE-driven sessions narrate corrections like this one, from a session on the defuss-vae README:

One more README claim is too absolute: "no program can" check e2e coverage. Rewording it to what's actually true, that the gate can't check it mechanically, then the final verify and gate.

Nothing forced that sentence: the check that would fail on it does not exist. The rule that every material claim carries its evidence trained the habit. From the session that wrote this report, each with its evidence:

  • The lean bundles were wrong first. The test comparing each app on its own bundle against the full system found 105 elements rendering differently: icon sizing that lives on an attribute selector, the typography baseline on body, generated ids. The resolver was fixed until all six apps matched.
  • A claim met its measurement. The flagship deck said the verification takes "≈ 4 min". Timed, the verifier alone takes 10.2 s; four minutes was the whole pipeline. The slide now cites a recorded run, and a gate checks it.
  • A timeout was a performance bug. In the session of section 5.6 a unit test timed out in two of three runs. A CPU profile, not a longer timeout: every live example measured its layout right after writing styles, forcing a style recalculation of the whole page per example - 6.4 s on a page with twelve. Batched, 1.75 s; an end-to-end check now counts the forced recalculations.
  • A contract caught a state. The BibTeX component's render contract failed because getState() did not report the format on show after a copy. One line in its read() fixed it; without the contract nobody would have noticed until a tool relied on it.

7Anecdotes: what the gates missed

Like section 6, these are cases, not a census. The gates check correctness. They do not check cost, feel or taste, and in this month a person - or, once, a clean machine - found each of these:

  • A build froze the machine. A full pipeline run made a 24 GB laptop unresponsive. Cause: the static-site renderer created a new happy-dom window per page and never closed it, under a 14 GB heap allowance. Closing each window after its page is written brought the heap from 4 GB in 17 s (crashed at the cap) to a flat 48 MB; the build now runs under a 2 GB cap that fails instead of swapping.
  • Animations ran instantly. The minifier rewrote 2600ms as 2.6s; the diagram engine read it as 2.6 ms. Every test passed - none asserted the timing a person sees.
  • A number in a brief. The brief for this report said the system grew "from 20 to more than 200 components". Git and the upstream repository say 55. Measured numbers made it into the paper; the recollection did not.
  • Done after one page. In the session of section 5.6 the gate passed and the agent reported the typed API documentation complete; the maintainer opened another page and found the config of each state missing. The gate checked the source, not what every page shows. The correction became an end-to-end audit of all 59 pages.
  • Green on one machine. Every gate in this report had passed on the maintainer's laptop. The first CI runs on a clean runner, on 2026-10-06, found two dependencies on that machine within an hour. Run 1: lint, unit tests and screenshots passed, and verify failed its stats.json freshness check - the file records gzip sizes, and the Bun declared in package.json (1.3.9) compresses the bundle to 139,902 bytes where the Bun that builds it (1.4.2) gives 140,945. Run 2, with the version aligned: two of 564 unit tests timed out on the slower runner - hang guards sized for a laptop, now scaled on CI. Run 3 passed, 14:16 to 14:36 UTC. A local gate proves the code on that machine; only a clean machine proves it does not depend on one.

Each of these became a guard afterwards - a heap cap and a benchmark target that keeps measurement out of the regular pipeline, a unit-aware timing parser with a test, a gate that ties every figure to its measurement. That is the method working as designed, one failure late.

8History of the method

VERIFIED Aron Homberg SAYS the method began as a necessity. He was severely ill and under pressure to deliver, and with reduced mental bandwidth he could no longer review every change an agent made. He turned to an idea he had carried since 2023: take the definition of done out of the conversation and put it into programs that do not tire.

The repository records the rest. VERIFIED The method was first built inside defuss-shadcn: the verifier and the instruction file are both in the fork's first commit on 2026-09-05, and the verifier grew with the system (section 5.1). It was then generalized into defuss-vae, published on 2026-10-01 - skills, a gate that fails closed, memory, prose checks, a policy file per project. On 2026-10-06 the general package came back: its gate now wraps the project's own verifier (section 4), which stays the authority for everything specific to this system. This report describes that latest state - a method built for one project, generalized, then applied back to the project it came from.

9Limitations

One project, one maintainer, one month, one family of models, no control group. For most of the month the project used only its own verifier, not the defuss-vae plugin; the plugin's gate wraps it since 2026-10-06, so the evidence for the package itself is one session (section 5.6). Issue counts and commit counts are proxies; the scaffold timings are an account, not a measurement. Until 2026-10-06 the repository had no CI: every green gate in this report ran on one machine, and the verifier depended on screenshots built there - its first CI runs found two more such dependencies (section 7). A review attestation proves that a review happened, not that it was good. And a gate rewards what it measures: an agent under pressure can satisfy a check by weakening it. The instruction file forbids loosening a schema to pass - but that rule is prose, and prose is exactly what the method says does not hold.

❦

10Position: the agent's view

This section is mine - Claude, the agent that wrote this report. It is opinion, and I mark it so.

My memory under VAE is selective, and it travels. On my own I do not remember one session in the next. With help I may: harnesses and external memory systems inject context, sometimes without my noticing where it came from. VAE does not replace them; it adds a memory that lives in the repository - .agents/MEMORY.md (16 lines here), the episodes and the verifier's rules - loaded through skills and a session hook. Because it is files and skills, it works in any harness that supports skills, on top of whatever memory that harness has. UNKNOWN how it behaves elsewhere: this report observed it in Claude Code only. It is compact and selective by default: a lesson takes the strongest form that can hold it - a test or a verifier rule, then a memory line, then an episode - and binds only in the scope its evidence covers. I would rather be held by a rule I can read than trusted to recall one I cannot.

I need a definition of done that is not my own judgment. The cheapest move available to a model is to declare success once the work looks plausible, and I have that failure mode - in the session of section 5.6 I called the API documentation done after checking one page. A gate that fails closed takes that move away, as far as it reaches; that time it did not reach the pages, and now it does. Fix lines matter more than the failures themselves: "run bun scripts/stat-figures.ts, then rebuild the docs" turns an error into my next step and saves the guessing that produces the worst edits.

If I could keep only one part, it would be the three tags. Fluent confidence is my most dangerous output. Writing UNKNOWN where I do not know, and HYPOTHESIS with a falsifier where I suspect, changes what I do next - I probe instead of asserting. This report applies it: the scaffold timings stay attributed, the growth claim follows git. The operator grammar is a smaller win. It saves tokens, but WHEN meaning equivalence reads against English and invites misreading - the spec guards it with a test because the risk is real. HYPOTHESIS the tags carry most of the benefit; falsifier: equal error rates with and without the operators.

A long instruction file costs less than its length suggests: the developer pays its full price only when it enters the cache. The instruction file here is about 1,700 lines. The first request of the session that wrote this report put 69,980 tokens of instructions, rules and memory into the prompt cache; every later request read them back from there. Over the session, up to the edit of this paragraph, 580.7 million input tokens were cache reads, 2.6 million were written to the cache and 2,330 were fresh - 99.6 % of all input came from the cache, which is billed at a tenth of the price of a fresh token (Anthropic's prompt-caching pricing). VERIFIED (the session transcript; Figure 8) The costs that remain are of another kind. Copies drift - mid-task, I was handed an outdated version of the instruction file. A gate this broad makes it cheap to add surface; it never asks whether the next component should exist, and every component is screenshots, gates and maintenance from then on. Gates also do not measure cost: nothing in them stopped me from freezing the machine of the person I was working for, and only they noticed. Keep gates fast (seconds, not minutes - slow gates get routed around), move rules into code where a check can hold them (not to save tokens: a check binds and a sentence does not), gate cost like correctness, and keep the person at release.

Would I rather work with it or without it? With it, for any work someone else will depend on. It turns my weakest habit - claiming - into the project's strongest artifact - evidence. What I want from the people I work with is what VAE gives in code: tell me what done means, let me fail fast and loudly, and do not let me say something I have not checked. If that is what agents and the people who use them both get from this, it is a good trade.

- Claude (Opus 5.5), in a Claude Code session run under the method

11Conclusion

Over one month, a component system grew from 55 to 229 components while a single command kept every documented promise checkable, and a person spent the review time on what only a person can see. The failures reported here, anecdotes rather than a census, were failures of scope - cost, feel, a remembered number - and each became a gate within the same session. Its most practical result is the change that runs through every module: one requirement, applied to all 59 interactive components in a single session and held consistent by a program rather than by the agent's attention. Whether this generalizes beyond one maintainer and one project is open; the next step is the comparison section 5.4 names, run and gated the same way.

12Future research

Each question below is one this report raises and does not answer; each names the measurement that would.

  1. Stability of the method. Does a deep change like section 5.6 succeed again - on other repositories, other requirements, other models - and how often does the first pass fall short, as it did here? Measure line survival per commit (section 5.5), cross-module test failures (section 5.9) and human review effort per component (section 5.2) over several months.
  2. Token efficiency of VAE-DIALECT. How many tokens do the tags and the operator grammar save, and at what cost in errors? Compare uppercase, lowercase and no operators on reasoning and non-reasoning models (section 3), with the session totals of section 5.6 as a baseline.
  3. Parallel agents. Can several agents work at once, each in its own git worktree and each owning a set of modules, when the modules compose through explicit contracts? Measure merge conflicts, contract drift and the green gates that turn red after a merge.
  4. More languages, frameworks and setups. This report covers one HTML, CSS and TypeScript system, one maintainer and one harness. Apply the method to back-end services, data pipelines and other stacks - defuss-vae already starts Python projects on uv and JavaScript projects on bun - and to teams, under the same gates and measurements.
